evidence: Mart. Cap. 3.310; Diom. p. 331 P. (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The later grammarians’ modus īnfīnītīvus, the term of every modern grammar: īnfīnītīvum āctīvum, passīvum, the active and passive infinitive (Traupman 229). Quintilian’s term is verbum īnfīnītum, “the unlimited verb” (see below).

evidence: Quint. 9.3.9: cum īnfīnītō verbō sit ūsus prō appellātiōne
Quint. 1.6.8: dummodo per eandem litteram in īnfīnītō exeant
terms.comment: Quintilian’s term, often with verbum left out: the form not limited by person or number. The older name; the grammars and the classroom use the later one.

phrases.latin: nostrum istud vīvere triste aspexī, cum īnfīnītō verbō sit ūsus prō appellātiōne
phrases.english: “I have seen that sad living of ours”, where he has used an infinitive in place of a noun

phrases.latin: Dīc īnfīnītīvum āctīvum hujus verbī, praesentī tempore.
phrases.english: Give the present active infinitive of this verb.

sources: Lewis & Short: infinitus · Lewis & Short: infinitivus
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency (printed page numbers): p. 225, p. 229, p. 247.
